Comparing methods and settings

Source: vignettes/compare.Rmd
compare.Rmd

Several choices come down to a comparison between configurations: retrieve against map_reduce for a corpus, smaller chunks against larger, top_k = 1 against more, and how much of each record the screener sees. You settle each one the same way. Build one arm per configuration, run all the arms on the same labelled questions several times, and read the report with its intervals.

vignette("evaluate") explains the parts: references and splits, arms, scorers, benchmarks, reports and judges. This guide uses them for five comparisons: readers, segmenters and chunk sizes, one setting swept over its values, screening settings, and a judge against people’s labels. Each runs offline on a stand-in model and ends in a report, with what that report shows and what it leaves open. The last section repeats the steps on your own documents.

Setting up 

library(harnessr)
old <- hr_options(verbose = FALSE, embedder = "lexical")
op <- options(digits = 3)
# Illustrative prices for a stand-in model. For a real model, use your
# provider's current prices.
hr_register_model("mock-model", context_window = 128000, max_output = 16384,
                  input_usd = 1, output_usd = 4)

The stand-in model’s id is mock-model, and its price gives each benchmark a cost you can compare. The corpus is twelve short annual reports. Each has six paragraphs, one topic each, and four questions about it. As in real reports, some sentences share a question’s words without answering it (“Export revenue rose with prices”), so ranking chunks by the question’s words can pick the wrong one:

co <- data.frame(
  place   = c("Ashford", "Bexley", "Carlow", "Dunmore", "Elstow", "Fenwick",
              "Garston", "Hollins", "Irvine", "Jarrow", "Kelso", "Larne"),
  revenue = c(45.2, 51.8, 38.9, 29.4, 61.3, 33.7, 48.5, 27.1, 55.6, 40.2, 36.4, 52.9),
  units   = c(12400, 9800, 15100, 7600, 11200, 8300, 13900, 6900, 10500, 14700, 9100, 12800),
  staff   = c(310, 275, 402, 198, 356, 221, 389, 167, 298, 344, 251, 377),
  exports = c(7, 12, 4, 9, 15, 6, 11, 3, 8, 14, 5, 10))

report <- function(r) paste(c(
  sprintf("%s annual report", r$place),
  sprintf(paste("Results. Revenue was %.1f million dollars in fiscal 2024. Analysts expect",
                "revenue to reach %.1f million dollars by 2026 if prices hold. Export",
                "revenue rose with prices."), r$revenue, round(r$revenue * 1.2, 1)),
  sprintf(paste("Operations. The plant in %s made %s units. Output was limited by a two week",
                "shutdown for repairs. A second line is planned for next year."),
          r$place, format(r$units, big.mark = ",")),
  sprintf(paste("People. Staff numbered %d at year end. Training hours per person doubled.",
                "Turnover fell for the third year."), r$staff),
  sprintf(paste("Trade. Exports rose %d percent. Most shipments went by sea. Units shipped",
                "abroad by the plant are counted separately."), r$exports),
  paste("Governance. The audit committee met four times. Staff representatives joined",
        "the board at year end.")),
  collapse = "\n\n")
docs <- setNames(vapply(seq_len(nrow(co)), function(i) report(co[i, ]), ""), co$place)

qs <- c(revenue = "What was revenue in fiscal 2024?",
        units   = "How many units did the plant make?",
        staff   = "How many staff were there at year end?",
        exports = "By how much did exports rise?")
grid_q <- expand.grid(topic = names(qs), place = co$place, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
answer_of <- function(place, topic) {
  r <- co[co$place == place, ]
  switch(topic, revenue = sprintf("%.1f million", r$revenue),
         units = format(r$units, big.mark = ","), staff = as.character(r$staff),
         exports = sprintf("%d percent", r$exports))
}
qa <- gr_qa_reference(
  questions = setNames(unname(qs[grid_q$topic]), paste(grid_q$place, grid_q$topic, sep = "_")),
  documents = unname(docs[grid_q$place]),
  answers   = unname(Map(answer_of, grid_q$place, grid_q$topic)),
  cluster   = grid_q$place,
  split     = ifelse(grid_q$place %in% co$place[1:4], "dev", "test"))
qa
#> <hr_reference> 48 item(s) in 12 cluster(s)
#>   splits: dev 16, test 32 
#>   hash: c3a742404b80

The first four reports form the dev split, kept for tuning. The other eight form the test split, and every reported comparison is scored on it. Each report is one cluster, because its four questions share its quirks. For a set of your own, hr_assign_splits() draws the split.

The stand-in reader answers from its prompt. It returns the sentence there that answers the question, or NOT_IN_DOCUMENT if the prompt lacks one. Like a real model, it does worse as its prompt grows: it misses a sentence it was shown with probability equal to the prompt’s length in characters over 6000.

pattern <- c(revenue = "Revenue was [0-9.]+ million dollars in fiscal 2024",
             units = "made [0-9,]+ units", staff = "Staff numbered [0-9]+",
             exports = "Exports rose [0-9]+ percent")
reader <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  seen <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) as.character(m$content), ""), collapse = " ")
  asked <- sub(".*Question", "", seen)
  topic <- names(pattern)[vapply(c("revenue", "units", "staff", "exports"), grepl,
                                 logical(1), x = asked, ignore.case = TRUE)][1]
  hit <- regmatches(seen, regexpr(pattern[[topic]], seen))
  if (!length(hit)) return("NOT_IN_DOCUMENT")
  if (runif(1) < nchar(seen) / 6000) return("The report does not say clearly.")
  paste0(hit, ".")
})

Which settings there are

A schema declares every setting a reader, segmenter or ingest step takes, with its type, default, range, tier and the evidence behind its default. gr_settings() returns the schema, and its print shows each setting’s tier and evidence status:

gr_settings("segment")
#> <hr_schema> 20 parameter(s)
#>   context_source             enum          advanced  untested  metadata|llm
#>   max_tokens                 integer       basic     untested  [32, 1e+06]
#>   overlap_tokens             integer       basic     untested  [0, f()]
#>   min_tokens                 integer       advanced  untested  [0, f()]
#>   method                     module_ref    basic     untested  
#>   separators                 string_vector advanced  untested  
#>   prefix_section             boolean       advanced  untested  
#>   semantic_window            integer       advanced  untested  [1, 10]
#>   semantic_percentile        number        advanced  untested  [50, 99.5]
#>   proposition_batch_tokens   integer       advanced  untested  [200, 4000]
#>   parallel                   boolean       advanced  untested  
#>   context_reply_tokens       integer       advanced  untested  [16, 4000]
#>   context_document_tokens    integer       advanced  untested  [100, 1e+06]
#>   proposition_reply_tokens   integer       advanced  untested  [100, 1e+06]
#>   semantic_threshold         enum          advanced  untested  percentile|texttiling
#>   table_packing              enum          advanced  untested  rows|grouped
#>   proposition_check          enum          advanced  untested  count|drop
#>   proposition_context_tokens integer       advanced  untested  [0, 2000]
#>   packing                    enum          advanced  untested  greedy|balanced
#>   runt_merge                 enum          advanced  untested  backward|both

The basic tier marks the few settings most comparisons vary. In the read schema those are reader, model, top_k, cite and verify. as.data.frame() adds each default and where it came from:

rs <- as.data.frame(gr_settings("read"))
rs[rs$name %in% c("top_k", "lexical_blend", "bm25_k1"), c("name", "default", "status", "source")]
#>             name default   status
#> 13         top_k       6 untested
#> 31       bm25_k1     1.5    cited
#> 33 lexical_blend     0.5 untested
#>                                                                                                                                            source
#> 13                                                                                         A common starting value for retrieval; not tuned here.
#> 31 Robertson and Zaragoza (2009), "The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond", give k1 between 1.2 and 2.0 as usual; not tuned here.
#> 33                                                                                          An even blend, set when the offline path was written.

Most defaults are untested: someone picked them without measuring them, which makes them worth comparing. You can give any setting in these schemas to gr_arm() in settings, which takes what answer_document() takes in ....

The rules every comparison here follows

  • Tune on dev, report on test. Choose settings by their dev results, and never report those results. A setting chosen on the test split and then reported on it is fitted to those questions, so part of its advantage is luck. hr_report() leaves dev rows out.
  • At least five runs, and ten when the report asks. A model asked the same question twice can answer differently. With fewer than five runs, hr_benchmark() warns and hr_report() gives no intervals. If run-to-run variance is above 10% of the total, the report’s notes say “use runs = 10”.
  • One governor for the whole benchmark. The default limits fit one read (400 calls). Size hr_governor() for arms x items x runs x calls per run, and afterwards check how much of it the benchmark used.
  • Read intervals. An arm ahead by 5 points with an interval from -3 to 13 has not been shown to be better.
  • Know the smallest difference the design can detect. hr_mdd() gives it before you run anything.

The test split here is 32 questions in 8 reports. If the two arms disagree on about 15% of questions and questions in one report are correlated at 0.1:

hr_mdd(32, n_clusters = 8, icc = 0.1, p_disc = 0.15)
#> <hr_mdd> 25.5 points at 80% power, one-sided alpha 0.025
#>   32 items in 8 clusters (m = 4, 4 after cv 0), ICC_D 0.1: DE 1.3, n_eff 24.6
#>   p_disc 0.15
hr_n_needed(0.05, m = 4, icc = 0.1, p_disc = 0.15)
#> <hr_n_needed> 5.0 points at 80% power, one-sided alpha 0.025
#>   n_eff 477 effective items; DE 1.3, so 624 items in 156 clusters of 4

No comparison below is designed to detect a difference smaller than about 25.5 points. A 5 point difference would need about 624 questions in 156 reports. At this size, a difference the report calls uncertain is not evidence that the arms are the same.

Readers on the same questions

Three readers run here, each with the segmentation it is usually paired with:

  • stuff sends the whole report in one request.
  • map_reduce reads 60-token chunks one by one and merges the answers.
  • retrieve sends the two 60-token chunks of sentences that rank highest.
readers <- list(
  gr_arm("fast", name = "stuff"),
  gr_arm("thorough", settings = list(max_tokens = 60, overlap_tokens = 0), name = "map_reduce"),
  gr_arm("fast", settings = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 2, method = "sentence",
                                 max_tokens = 60), name = "retrieve"))
gov <- hr_governor(max_calls = 3 * 32 * 10 * 8, max_cost_usd = 1)
b_read <- hr_benchmark(readers, qa, runs = 10, client = reader,
                       scorer = gr_scorer_answer(), governor = gov)
b_read
#> <hr_bench> 3 arm(s) x 32 item(s) in 8 cluster(s) x 10 run(s); split test; scorer answer_contains
#>  arm        accuracy runs wrong failed budget_stop usd   
#>  stuff      0.847    320  49    0      0           0.0972
#>  map_reduce 0.906    320  30    0      0           0.2430
#>  retrieve   0.894    320  34    0      0           0.0686
#>   cost: $0.4088 across mock-model, prices as of 2026-11
#>   Descriptive only: accuracy is the mean over runs within each item, then over labelled items, with no interval.
hr_trace_summary(attr(b_read, "trace"))[, c("calls", "tokens_in", "tokens_out")]
#>   calls tokens_in tokens_out
#> 1  1920    304730      26029

Each arm runs 10 times. With runs = 5 the report’s notes said “Run-to-run variance is 81% of the total, above 10%: use runs = 10.”, and the rule on runs is to follow that note. The governor allows 8 calls per run for each of 3 arms, 32 questions and 10 runs: 7,680 in all. That is more than map_reduce needs on reports this short, and the trace records 1,920 calls.

r_read <- hr_report(b_read, B = 200)
r_read$accuracy[, c("arm", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>          arm estimate lower upper
#> 1      stuff    0.847 0.783 0.894
#> 2 map_reduce    0.906 0.870 0.933
#> 3   retrieve    0.894 0.780 0.952
r_read$contrasts[, c("arm1", "arm2", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>         arm1       arm2 estimate   lower    upper
#> 1      stuff map_reduce  -0.0594 -0.1140 -0.00472
#> 2      stuff   retrieve  -0.0469 -0.1293  0.03555
#> 3 map_reduce   retrieve   0.0125 -0.0711  0.09610
r_read$simultaneous[, c("arm1", "arm2", "estimate", "lower", "upper", "critical")]
#>         arm1       arm2 estimate   lower   upper critical
#> 1      stuff map_reduce  -0.0594 -0.1269 0.00816     2.92
#> 2      stuff   retrieve  -0.0469 -0.1487 0.05497     2.92
#> 3 map_reduce   retrieve   0.0125 -0.0908 0.11580     2.92
r_read$cost[, c("arm", "usd_per_item", "tokens_per_item")]
#>          arm usd_per_item tokens_per_item
#> 1      stuff     0.000304             268
#> 2 map_reduce     0.000759             588
#> 3   retrieve     0.000214             178

map_reduce has the highest estimate, 0.906, against 0.894 for retrieve and 0.847 for stuff. The intervals below do not show that it is more accurate than either.

contrasts gives each pair its own 95% interval. For stuff against map_reduce that interval, -0.114 to -0.005, narrowly excludes 0. But three pairs were compared, and with three intervals at 95% each, the chance that at least one excludes 0 by luck is higher than 5%.

simultaneous gives intervals that hold for all three pairs at once (max-t). Its critical column is the multiplier of the standard error, 2.92 here. A single pair’s interval uses a smaller one, so each simultaneous interval is wider. There the same difference runs from -0.127 to 0.008, which includes 0, and this design has not shown that stuff is worse. If you compare more than two arms and named no one pair before the run, read simultaneous.

map_reduce against retrieve is 0.013, from -0.091 to 0.116 at once, so no difference is shown. The minimum detectable difference is 25.5 points: this design would show a true difference of that size 80% of the time. It would show a true difference of 1 point much less often, though not never, so this result does not say the two readers are equally accurate.

The cost gap is large. map_reduce sends 588 tokens per question against 178 for retrieve, and costs 3.5 times as much. You decide whether an unproven point is worth that; the report informs the decision and does not make it. The stand-in is built to miss more in long prompts, so these figures say nothing about any real model. They show how to read the report.

Segmenters and chunk sizes

Test a segmenter first at no cost, then with a model. Two free measures come before any benchmark.

Boundaries against the topics

Each report’s six paragraphs are its topics, so the paragraphs serve as a reference segmentation. gr_seg_boundaries() maps a segmentation to sentence boundaries. gr_seg_pk() and gr_seg_windowdiff() measure how far a chunking’s boundaries fall from the reference’s: 0 means the same boundaries, and lower is better. The grid crosses three segmenters with two sizes:

seg_grid <- expand.grid(method = c("fixed", "sentence", "paragraph"),
                        max_tokens = c(40, 80), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
seg_grid$name <- paste(seg_grid$method, seg_grid$max_tokens, sep = "_")
dev_docs <- docs[co$place[1:4]]

boundary_error <- function(method, max_tokens) {
  per_doc <- vapply(dev_docs, function(d) {
    ref <- gr_seg_boundaries(strsplit(d, "\n\n")[[1]], d)
    hyp <- gr_seg_boundaries(gr_segment(d, list(method = method, max_tokens = max_tokens)), d)
    c(pk = gr_seg_pk(ref, hyp), windowdiff = gr_seg_windowdiff(ref, hyp))
  }, numeric(2))
  round(rowMeans(per_doc), 3)
}
cbind(seg_grid["name"], t(mapply(boundary_error, seg_grid$method, seg_grid$max_tokens)))
#>                     name    pk windowdiff
#> fixed           fixed_40 0.444      0.444
#> sentence     sentence_40 0.722      0.722
#> paragraph   paragraph_40 0.194      0.222
#> fixed.1         fixed_80 0.500      0.500
#> sentence.1   sentence_80 0.556      0.556
#> paragraph.1 paragraph_80 0.278      0.278

A paragraph here is about 30 tokens. At 40 tokens the paragraph segmenter makes most chunks one paragraph and has the lowest error, Pk 0.194. At 80 tokens it packs two paragraphs into a chunk and misses the boundary between them (0.278). The sentence segmenter packs sentences across paragraph ends and does worst: 0.722 at 40 tokens, worse than fixed windows (0.444), which ignore the text.

The two measures differ only for paragraph_40 (0.194 and 0.222), because WindowDiff also counts a window in which both have a boundary but not the same number. Both measure where chunk edges fall. Neither tells you whether a reader will find the answer.

Whether the answer is in the chunks retrieved

gr_seg_recall() ranks each segmentation’s chunks for each question the way the retrieve reader does, then counts the questions whose answer is in the first k chunks. With the lexical embedder it calls no model:

seg_specs <- setNames(lapply(seq_len(nrow(seg_grid)), function(i) {
  list(method = seg_grid$method[i], max_tokens = seg_grid$max_tokens[i])
}), seg_grid$name)
rec <- gr_seg_recall(qa, seg_specs, k = c(1, 2), split = "dev")
rec[rec$k == 1, c("segmenter", "hits", "questions", "recall", "no_chunk", "chunks")]
#>       segmenter hits questions recall no_chunk chunks
#> 1      fixed_40    8        16   0.50        0    5.0
#> 3   sentence_40   12        16   0.75        0    7.0
#> 5  paragraph_40   12        16   0.75        0    6.5
#> 7      fixed_80   12        16   0.75        0    3.0
#> 9   sentence_80    8        16   0.50        0    4.0
#> 11 paragraph_80   12        16   0.75        0    3.0

With one chunk retrieved, four settings put the answer first for 12 of the 16 dev questions, and fixed_40 and sentence_80 do so for 8. no_chunk is 0 throughout, so no chunk edge cut an answer in two. The misses come from the ranking: a chunk that shares the question’s words (such as “Export revenue rose with prices”) can outrank the one that answers it. attr(rec, "ranks") gives the rank of the answering chunk for every question. Neither measure called a model.

A grid of arms on dev, then one comparison on test

Next the same grid becomes arms, one per row. Each arm is the retrieve reader with top_k = 1 and that row’s segmenter and size, and the arms run on the dev split:

seg_arms <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(seg_grid)), function(i) {
  gr_arm("fast", settings = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = 1,
                                 method = seg_grid$method[i],
                                 max_tokens = seg_grid$max_tokens[i]),
         name = seg_grid$name[i])
})
b_seg_dev <- hr_benchmark(seg_arms, qa, runs = 5, client = reader, split = "dev",
                          scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                          governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 6 * 16 * 5, max_cost_usd = 1))
b_seg_dev
#> <hr_bench> 6 arm(s) x 16 item(s) in 4 cluster(s) x 5 run(s); split dev; scorer answer_contains
#>  arm          accuracy dev   runs wrong failed budget_stop usd   
#>  fixed_40     -        0.475 80   2     40     0           0.0146
#>  sentence_40  -        0.713 80   3     20     0           0.0133
#>  paragraph_40 -        0.725 80   2     20     0           0.0136
#>  fixed_80     -        0.688 80   5     20     0           0.0178
#>  sentence_80  -        0.500 80   0     40     0           0.0151
#>  paragraph_80 -        0.688 80   5     20     0           0.0158
#>   cost: $0.0902 across mock-model, prices as of 2026-11
#>   480 row(s) on the dev split are not reportable; their accuracy is the dev column alone.
#>   Descriptive only: accuracy is the mean over runs within each item, then over labelled items, with no interval.

The print shows accuracy only in the dev column, and hr_report() would refuse these rows. On dev, paragraph_40 scores highest at 0.725, narrowly above sentence_40 at 0.713. The two arms whose recall at 1 was 0.50 score lowest (0.475 and 0.500). The best of six close dev scores is partly luck, so you confirm it on test. There it faces the paragraph segmenter at 80 tokens, the other size of the same segmenter:

b_seg <- hr_benchmark(seg_arms[match(c("paragraph_40", "paragraph_80"), seg_grid$name)], qa,
                      runs = 10, client = reader, scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 2 * 32 * 10, max_cost_usd = 1))
r_seg <- hr_report(b_seg, B = 200)
r_seg$accuracy[, c("arm", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>            arm estimate lower upper
#> 1 paragraph_40    0.834 0.695 0.917
#> 2 paragraph_80    0.703 0.666 0.738
r_seg$contrasts[, c("arm1", "arm2", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>           arm1         arm2 estimate  lower upper
#> 1 paragraph_40 paragraph_80    0.131 0.0132 0.249

This benchmark also runs 10 times, since at 5 runs its notes put run-to-run variance at 15% of the total. On test, paragraph_40 scores 0.834 and paragraph_80 0.703. The difference of 0.131 has an interval from 0.013 to 0.249, which excludes 0. You can report it because it is one contrast, and both arms were chosen on dev before anyone saw their test results. The interval still has the width that 8 reports allow: the gain could be anything from 1 to 25 points.

One setting swept over its values

top_k sets how many chunks retrieve sends. More chunks raise the chance that the answer is among them, and they make the prompt longer. The sweep runs on dev:

top_k_arms <- lapply(c(1, 2, 4), function(k) {
  gr_arm("fast", settings = list(reader = "retrieve", top_k = k, method = "sentence",
                                 max_tokens = 40), name = paste0("top_k_", k))
})
b_k_dev <- hr_benchmark(top_k_arms, qa, runs = 5, client = reader, split = "dev",
                        scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                        governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 3 * 16 * 5, max_cost_usd = 1))
b_k_dev
#> <hr_bench> 3 arm(s) x 16 item(s) in 4 cluster(s) x 5 run(s); split dev; scorer answer_contains
#>  arm     accuracy dev   runs wrong failed budget_stop usd   
#>  top_k_1 -        0.738 80   1     20     0           0.0133
#>  top_k_2 -        0.950 80   4      0     0           0.0153
#>  top_k_4 -        0.912 80   7      0     0           0.0199
#>   cost: $0.0485 across mock-model, prices as of 2026-11
#>   240 row(s) on the dev split are not reportable; their accuracy is the dev column alone.
#>   Descriptive only: accuracy is the mean over runs within each item, then over labelled items, with no interval.

top_k = 2 is highest on dev, at 0.950. top_k = 1 misses the questions whose answer ranks second. top_k = 4 gives the stand-in a longer prompt, which it reads worse. On test the chosen value faces top_k = 4, the value nearer the default of 6:

b_k <- hr_benchmark(top_k_arms[2:3], qa, runs = 10, client = reader,
                    scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                    governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 2 * 32 * 10, max_cost_usd = 1))
r_k <- hr_report(b_k, B = 200)
r_k$contrasts[, c("arm1", "arm2", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>      arm1    arm2 estimate  lower upper
#> 1 top_k_2 top_k_4   0.0687 0.0179  0.12
r_k$cost[, c("arm", "usd_per_item", "tokens_per_item")]
#>       arm usd_per_item tokens_per_item
#> 1 top_k_2     0.000192             155
#> 2 top_k_4     0.000250             213

With 10 runs (at 5, the notes put run-to-run variance at 79% of the total), top_k = 2 is 6.9 points more accurate than top_k = 4 on test. The interval runs from 1.8 to 12.0 points, and top_k = 2 sends 155 tokens per question instead of 213.

The difference is far below the 25.5-point minimum detectable difference above, and the interval still excludes 0. The two figures do not contradict each other. The 25.5 points is the true difference this design would detect 80% of the time, on an assumed disagreement of 15% and a correlation of 0.1. It is neither the width of an interval nor a floor under what can be shown: a smaller true difference is detected less often, not never. The interval rests on what these two arms did. Plan with values measured in a pilot on dev, and read the result from the report.

Screening settings

An arm can be any function, so you compare a screening setting the same way. Here a screener checks 16 records of hand-hygiene studies for randomised comparisons. Every record opens with the same background, and the sentence that settles it comes second, third or fourth, so a screener shown too little of a record cannot decide:

rec_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "compare-records")
dir.create(rec_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
set.seed(4)
n <- 16
design <- rep(c("randomly assigned", "followed an existing cohort of"), length.out = n)
lead <- c("Hand hygiene in hospital wards has been studied for decades.",
          "Compliance varies between units and shifts.",
          "Audits rarely capture night work.")
where <- rep(1:3, length.out = n)
records <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
  method <- sprintf("We %s %d nurses across %d wards.", design[i], sample(80:300, 1),
                    sample(4:12, 1))
  body <- append(lead, method, after = where[i])
  paste(c(sprintf("Study %02d.", i), body, "Infections were recorded for six months."),
        collapse = " ")
}, "")
paths <- file.path(rec_dir, sprintf("study%02d.txt", seq_len(n)))
for (i in seq_len(n)) writeLines(records[i], paths[i])

protocol <- gr_protocol("hygiene", question = "Does hand hygiene training reduce infections?",
                        include = "Reports a randomised comparison",
                        exclude = "Is an observational study")
screens <- hr_reference(setNames(as.list(paths), sprintf("s%02d", seq_len(n))),
                        labels = ifelse(grepl("randomly", design), "include", "exclude"),
                        cluster = sprintf("batch%d", rep(1:4, each = 4)), split = "test")

The stand-in screener decides from the allocation sentence if the excerpt it was shown holds that sentence, and says unclear otherwise. Each value of screen_tokens, the cap on what the screener is shown, gets one arm. Each run screens one record through gr_screen(), on the run’s trace and at its draw index:

screener <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  shown <- paste(vapply(messages, function(m) as.character(m$content), ""), collapse = " ")
  reply <- function(d, why, crit) {
    sprintf('{"decision":"%s","reason":"%s","criterion":%s,"quote":null}', d, why, crit)
  }
  if (grepl("randomly assigned", shown)) {
    return(reply("include", "Randomised.", '"Reports a randomised comparison"'))
  }
  if (grepl("existing cohort", shown)) {
    return(reply("exclude", "Observational.", '"Is an observational study"'))
  }
  reply("unclear", "The excerpt does not say how nurses were allocated.", "null")
})
screen_arm <- function(tokens) {
  hr_arm(paste0("tokens_", tokens), function(item, ctx) {
    gr_screen(item, protocol, client = ctx$client, screen_tokens = ctx$params$tokens,
              trace = ctx$trace)$table$decision
  }, params = list(tokens = tokens))
}
b_scr <- hr_benchmark(list(screen_arm(40), screen_arm(80)), screens, runs = 5,
                      client = screener,
                      governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 2 * 16 * 5, max_cost_usd = 1))
table(b_scr$arm, b_scr$outcome)
#>            
#>             exclude include unclear
#>   tokens_40       0      15      65
#>   tokens_80      40      40       0
r_scr <- hr_report(b_scr, B = 200)
r_scr$accuracy[, c("arm", "estimate", "lower", "upper")]
#>         arm estimate  lower upper
#> 1 tokens_40    0.188 0.0589  0.46
#> 2 tokens_80    1.000 0.7136  1.00
r_scr$cost[, c("arm", "usd_per_item", "tokens_per_item")]
#>         arm usd_per_item tokens_per_item
#> 1 tokens_40     0.000568             352
#> 2 tokens_80     0.000585             363

At 40 tokens the allocation sentence fits in the excerpt for 3 of the 16 records, and the screener says unclear about the other 13. Accuracy is 0.188, with an interval from 0.059 to 0.460, against 1.000 at 80 tokens. That second interval, 0.714 to 1.000, is Korn and Graubard’s, one-sided because every run was right. The cap saves little, 352 tokens per record against 363, since the instructions and criteria are most of each request.

This guide counts an unclear decision as wrong. It is not an exclusion, since a person settles it, but it costs that person a look. A scorer that counts it another way takes a few lines with hr_scorer().

A judge against people’s labels

Some outputs need a judge. A judge is a model, and you check its decisions against people before its scores mean anything. A pairwise judge says which of two texts answers better. Its labels come from a pairwise sheet: two texts per row, in an order drawn for that row. An opaque key keeps the order, so the person labelling cannot tell which text is which candidate.

Here 180 pairs set the right sentence against a wrong one (the 2026 forecast in place of the 2024 figure), or two right sentences against each other:

right <- sprintf("Revenue was %.1f million dollars in fiscal 2024.", co$revenue)
wrong <- sprintf("Revenue will reach %.1f million dollars by 2026.", round(co$revenue * 1.2, 1))
pick <- rep(seq_len(nrow(co)), length.out = 180)
kind <- rep(c("A", "B", "tie"), each = 60)
pairs <- data.frame(
  item_id = sprintf("p%03d", 1:180),
  question = "What was revenue in fiscal 2024?",
  candidate_a = ifelse(kind == "B", wrong[pick], right[pick]),
  candidate_b = ifelse(kind == "A", wrong[pick], right[pick]))
sheet_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "pairs.csv")
sheet <- gr_label_sheet("pairwise", pairs, path = sheet_path)
head(sheet[, c("item_id", "text_1", "text_2", "order_key")], 3)
#>   item_id                                           text_1
#> 1    p001 Revenue will reach 54.2 million dollars by 2026.
#> 2    p002 Revenue was 51.8 million dollars in fiscal 2024.
#> 3    p003 Revenue was 38.9 million dollars in fiscal 2024.
#>                                             text_2
#> 1 Revenue was 45.2 million dollars in fiscal 2024.
#> 2 Revenue will reach 62.2 million dollars by 2026.
#> 3 Revenue will reach 46.7 million dollars by 2026.
#>                                            order_key
#> 1 pk74fe8ffc5d402f4cab21b935c58cde250f4d0f04721af381
#> 2 pkca3ed8308d8da28a3560dd6164f3362c8c59210c37c6614e
#> 3 pk861aaaba18ad688ed514afc499ed67224d091e42cf6b22f9

A person fills preferred with 1, 2 or tie for each row as shown. Here the code below simulates the filling: the text with the 2024 figure is preferred, and two right texts are a tie.

filled <- read.csv(sheet_path, fileEncoding = "UTF-8-BOM")
has_2024 <- function(x) grepl("fiscal 2024", x)
filled$preferred <- ifelse(has_2024(filled$text_1) & has_2024(filled$text_2), "tie",
                           ifelse(has_2024(filled$text_1), "1", "2"))
write.csv(filled, sheet_path, row.names = FALSE, na = "")
labels <- gr_read_labels(sheet_path, "pairwise")
table(shown_first = labels$shown_first, preferred = labels$preferred)
#>            preferred
#> shown_first  A  B tie
#>           A 28 25  29
#>           B 32 35  31

gr_read_labels() uses the key to turn each answer back into candidate order, so preferred is A, B or tie whichever text was shown first. A key that was edited, lost or pasted onto another row is an error of class gr_bad_labels.

The judge sees each pair in both orders. This stand-in judge prefers the text with the 2024 figure, but a quarter of the time it picks whichever text it was shown first:

judge_cl <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  txt <- messages[[2]]$content
  a <- grepl("Candidate A:\n[^\n]*fiscal 2024", txt)
  b <- grepl("Candidate B:\n[^\n]*fiscal 2024", txt)
  v <- if (runif(1) < 0.25) "A" else if (a && b) "tie" else if (a) "A" else "B"
  sprintf('{"verdict": "%s", "reason": "Compared."}', v)
})
rubric <- "Which candidate gives fiscal 2024 revenue?"
# Illustrative prices for a stand-in model. For a real model, use your
# provider's current prices.
hr_register_model("mock-judge", context_window = 128000, max_output = 4096,
                  input_usd = 1, output_usd = 4)
set.seed(5)
verdicts <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(pairs)), function(i) {
  j <- hr_judge(c(A = pairs$candidate_a[i], B = pairs$candidate_b[i]), judge_cl,
                mode = "pairwise", model = "mock-judge", rubric = rubric)
  if (identical(j$outcome, "answered")) j$value else NA_character_
}, "")
table(verdicts, useNA = "ifany")
#> verdicts
#>    A    B  tie <NA> 
#>   46   47   29   58

A verdict that changes with the order is unresolved, recorded as NA. With positive = "A", hr_judge_validate() measures how well the judge finds the pairs where candidate A is better. A tie and a B both count as negative:

cfg_pair <- hr_judge_config("mock-judge", rubric, mode = "pairwise")
v_pair <- hr_judge_validate(cfg_pair, data.frame(judge = verdicts, human = labels$preferred),
                            positive = "A", B = 200)
v_pair
#> <hr_judge_validation> config 9c12c6f5550d (pairwise, mock-judge)
#>   items: 180 labelled (60 positive, 120 negative), 58 unresolved, 0 dropped
#>   kappa:       0.814 [0.719, 0.897]
#>   sensitivity: 0.767 [0.646, 0.856], n = 60, half-width 0.105
#>   specificity: 1.000 [0.969, 1.000], n = 120
#>   swap inconsistency: 0.322 [0.258, 0.394], 58 of 180

The judge finds 0.767 of the 60 pairs where people preferred A, with an interval from 0.646 to 0.856. It never prefers A where they did not (specificity 1.000). Its swap inconsistency is 0.322: on 58 of 180 pairs the verdict changed with the order. Those pairs count as not preferring A, as a scorer would count them, and they are why sensitivity is low. A judge whose verdict changes on a third of pairs needs a better rubric or model before you use its scores. With positive = "A" a tie is negative, so a judge that calls a tie where people preferred A has missed it.

When the judge is the model it grades

A model grading its own answers can favour them. hr_scorer_judge() takes the judge’s model in judge_model (the configuration’s by default). hr_benchmark() marks each run whose requests went to that same model in self_judged. It refuses no run, and the report says so. Here the grade judge runs on mock-model, the model the arm reads with. Its validation record is simulated, as in vignette("evaluate"):

cfg_grade <- hr_judge_config("mock-model", "Does the response give the reference's answer?",
                             mode = "grade")
set.seed(3)
human <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(60, 60))
v_grade <- hr_judge_validate(cfg_grade, data.frame(judge = ifelse(runif(120) < 0.9, human, !human),
                                                   human = human), B = 200)
grader <- hr_mock_client(function(messages, params) {
  txt <- messages[[2]]$content
  block <- function(head) regmatches(txt, regexec(paste0(head, ":\n([^\n]*)"), txt))[[1]][2]
  ok <- grepl(block("Reference answer"), block("Response to grade"), fixed = TRUE)
  sprintf('{"verdict": "%s", "reason": "Compared."}', if (ok) "pass" else "fail")
})
judged <- hr_benchmark(readers[3], qa, runs = 10, client = reader,
                       scorer = hr_scorer_judge(cfg_grade, v_grade, grader),
                       governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 32 * 10, max_cost_usd = 1))
table(judged$self_judged, useNA = "ifany")
#> 
#> TRUE 
#>  320
cat(hr_report(judged, B = 200)$notes, sep = "\n")
#> 320 of 320 runs were graded by a judge on the arm's own model (retrieve: 320). A model grading its own output can favour it; compare with a judge on another model, or with human labels (hr_judge_ppi()).
#> More than 5% of the cost of retrieve rests on estimated token counts; read its cost as approximate.
#> Cost, pass^k, frontier share and rank intervals come from the cluster bootstrap, which can undercover below 300 items or 30 clusters; read them as rough.
#> The frontier share (how often an arm is on the cost-accuracy frontier over resamples) is an extension, not a published standard.

All 320 runs (32 questions times 10) are marked self_judged, and the first note says so. At 5 runs the notes put run-to-run variance at 82% of the total and asked for 10, so this benchmark runs 10 times. At 10 runs the notes no longer ask for more.

judge_model = "mock-judge" would mark the same runs FALSE. A run with no model request is NA. The match is exact: if the provider names its model differently from the one you asked for, give the served model id.

Reading a comparison honestly

Each of the five comparisons above ends in a report, and the reports share the same limits.

  • Read the interval of the difference, not the two accuracies. A contrast whose interval covers 0 has not shown a difference. With more than two arms, read simultaneous unless one pair was named before the run.
  • Compare the result with the minimum detectable difference. At 32 questions in 8 reports, this design would usually miss a real gain of 5 points. hr_n_needed() gives the number of questions that would show it.
  • Report only test results. The grids and sweeps above were read on dev. One setting was chosen there, and only that setting and one comparator ran on test: paragraph_40 against paragraph_80, and top_k = 2 against top_k = 4. If you report the best of six dev arms as if it were one planned comparison, you overstate it.
  • Five runs is the minimum. If the report’s notes say run-to-run variance is more than 10% of the total, use 10. At 5 runs the notes for the reader, segmenter, top_k and judge benchmarks on test all said so (81%, 15%, 79% and 82%), so those benchmarks run 10 times.
  • Size the governor for the whole benchmark and compare its limit with the calls the trace records. A run stopped by a limit is counted wrong.
  • Treat the free measures as clues. Pk, WindowDiff and recall at k suggest why an arm may do well. Only the benchmark shows whether it does.
  • Trust a judge’s scores only as far as its validation. Validate the judge against blind labels, say when it graded its own model, and correct judge-scored accuracy with hr_judge_ppi().

On your own documents

Here are the same steps on real documents with a real model. Nothing in this section runs when the guide is built. Results go to a directory you name. This example uses the per-user data directory, never the package’s own folder:

out <- file.path(tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "data"), "compare")
dir.create(out, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# 1. Questions about your documents, one row each, labelled by a person.
questions <- read.csv("my-questions.csv")   # columns: document, question
gr_label_sheet("qa", questions, path = file.path(out, "qa-labels.csv"))
# ... a person fills the sheet ...
lab <- gr_read_labels(file.path(out, "qa-labels.csv"), "qa", items = questions)
# Whole documents to dev or test; the shares are yours to choose.
lab <- hr_assign_splits(lab, props = c(dev = 0.3, test = 0.7), seed = 2026)$items
qa_own <- gr_qa_reference(
  questions = setNames(lab$question, lab$item_id), documents = lab$document,
  answers = as.list(ifelse(lab$answerable, lab$answer, NA)),
  unanswerable = lab$item_id[!lab$answerable], split = lab$split)

# 2. Free measures on dev: which segmentations put answers in the top chunks.
gr_seg_recall(qa_own, seg_specs, k = c(1, 3, 5), split = "dev")

# 3. The arms, tuned on dev.
cl <- hr_client()
dev <- hr_benchmark(top_k_arms, qa_own, runs = 5, client = cl, split = "dev",
                    scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                    governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 5000, max_cost_usd = 20))
dev

# 4. The arm chosen on dev against the current default on test, then the
#    report. Set `chosen` to the arm with the best dev accuracy in step 3.
chosen <- top_k_arms[[2]]
current <- gr_arm("fast", settings = list(reader = "retrieve", method = "sentence",
                                          max_tokens = 40), name = "top_k_default")
n_test <- sum(qa_own$split == "test")
hr_mdd(n_test, n_clusters = length(unique(qa_own$cluster[qa_own$split == "test"])),
       icc = 0.1, p_disc = 0.15)
# Use runs = 10 if the report's notes say run-to-run variance is above 10%.
test <- hr_benchmark(list(chosen, current), qa_own, runs = 5, client = cl,
                     scorer = gr_scorer_answer(),
                     governor = hr_governor(max_calls = 2 * n_test * 5 * 2, max_cost_usd = 20))
rpt <- hr_report(test)
rpt

# 5. Keep the results with the run, outside the package.
saveRDS(test, file.path(out, "test-bench.rds"))
writeLines(as_json(rpt), file.path(out, "test-report.json"))

max_calls and max_cost_usd above are examples. Set them from the number of arms, test questions, runs and calls per run (gr_readers() lists each reader’s calls), with room to spare.
